paper.title: Back to the countryside? Remote work and counterurbanisation in Denmark and Sweden
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no statistical-agency project number are given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Labour Force Survey data and actual work-from-home claims, via Javakhishvili-Larsen et al. (2026)
Statistics Denmark's municipality classification into five groups (Capital City Area, Metropolitan, Provincial, Commuter, Rural)
registers.role: geography / sample frame: origin and destination classification

registers.name_in_paper: Swedish four-type municipality classification (MT1 metropolitan, MT2 urban, MT3 rural/countryside, MT4 sparsely populated rural), following Westlund et al. (2014), Naldi et al. (2021), Rex and Westlund (2024)
registers.role: geography / sample frame: origin and destination classification

registers.name_in_paper: Municipal house prices (2023-adjusted), average housing prices per square meter
registers.role: controls: locational control in the origin municipality

linkages: Individuals' registered residential moves linked to origin municipality o and destination municipality d, which are then classified by urbanisation type (Denmark: five Statistics Denmark groups; Sweden: four municipality types, with the two rural types merged into 197 municipalities).
WFH probability assigned to individuals from Javakhishvili-Larsen et al. (2026), built on Labour Force Survey data and actual work-from-home claims, reflecting occupational flexibility.
Average municipal house prices (2023-fixed) in the origin municipality z linked to the individual observation.
Shortest travel distance between the centres of origin and destination municipalities attached to each move.

sample.universe: All residents of Denmark and of Sweden aged 24-74 in primary employment (secondary jobs excluded), 2014-2023, whose origin municipality is in the Copenhagen or Stockholm capital city area
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (individual i in migration year t)
selection_rules: All residents in both countries covered by the Danish and Swedish statistical agencies' longitudinal micro-register data.

Restrict to individuals aged 24-74 (lower bound: most people remain in the parental home until their mid-twenties; upper bound: substantial labour-market participation beyond the statutory retirement age of 69).
Restrict to individuals in primary employment, excluding secondary jobs.
Panel period 2014-2023, beginning in 2014 when both economies had recovered from the 2008-2009 financial crisis.
Origin municipality in the Capital City Area (Denmark: 24 CCA municipalities with job accessibility above 200,000; Sweden: Stockholm metropolitan area, 24 municipalities).
Only the last recorded residential move for each individual in a calendar year is used, cross-checked against the subsequent year's address.
DV2: further restricted to CCA out-migrants; DV3: to CCA-to-rural movers; DV4: to CCA-to-urban movers.
Period-specific models (Tables 7 and 8) restrict the pooled years to 2014-2019, 2020-2021 or 2022-2023.
sample.n_observations: Table 3 (DV1): 4,686,932 Denmark / 9,061,281 Sweden; Table 4 (DV2): 95,039 / 145,852; Table 5 (DV3): 49,265 / 62,209; Table 6 (DV4): 45,774 / 83,643. Tables 7 and 8 print no observation counts. (Table 3 prints the counts as '4686,932' and '9061,281'.)

construction_notes: DV1 and DV2 are binary and measure the last residential movement to the destination municipality during the migration year; footnote 3: only the last recorded move per individual per calendar year is used, validated by cross-checking the next year's address.

Denmark: rural destinations = Commuter (hinterland) plus Rural municipalities, included together because of their similar socioeconomic characteristics; other urban = Metropolitan plus Provincial municipalities.
Sweden: the two rural municipality groups (MT3 rural areas/countryside, MT4 sparsely populated rural areas) are merged into one group of 197 municipalities.
DV3 and DV4 are logarithmic transformations of the migration distance, which normalises skewed distributions and reduces the influence of extreme values.
Distance is measured as the shortest travel distance between the centres of origin and destination municipalities, based on official definitions.

WFH Probability ranges 0.02-0.915 and measures each individual's likelihood of remote work from occupational flexibility (Javakhishvili-Larsen et al. 2026, Labour Force Survey data and actual work-from-home claims).

House prices are municipal averages per square meter, fixed at 2023 prices, for the origin municipality; housing types (detached houses versus flats) are not controlled for and prices are used as a proxy.

Age groups: 24-34 (reference), 35-49, 50-64, 65+; family structure: single (reference), married, living together; education: primary (reference) to long higher; sector: private (reference), public; industry: primary and industry (reference), service, business services, public, other private; occupational skill: manual skilled (reference), high skilled, service skilled; wage quartiles 1st (reference) to 4th.
Periods: pre-pandemic / pre-COVID 2014-2019, pandemic 2020-2021, post-pandemic / post-COVID 2022-2023.
Logistic models report post-estimation average marginal effects, to be interpreted as times 100, i.e. in percentage points; odds ratios and robust standard errors are said to be available on request.

links.pointer_quote: In Denmark, higher work-from-home (WFH) probability paradoxically reduces CCA-to-rural migration, reinforcing metropolitan attachment, a pattern intensified during the pandemic.

claims.statement: Among Danish CCA residents, a higher work-from-home probability is associated with a lower probability of migrating from the Copenhagen capital city area to a rural municipality (2014-2023).

definition.value: Each individual's likelihood of remote work, ranging 0.02-0.915, reflecting occupational flexibility; taken from Javakhishvili-Larsen et al. (2026) using Labour Force Survey data and actual work-from-home claims. Enters the models as the continuous regressor WFH_it (coefficient beta_1).

timing.value: measured for individual i in migration year t, i.e. contemporaneously with the migration outcome

outcome.label: DV1: Migration Status (CCA vs. Rural), Denmark

definition.value: Binary dependent variable differentiating individuals who remain in the Copenhagen Capital City Area (0) from those relocating to rural areas (1). It measures the last residential movement to the destination municipality during the migration year. Rural destinations comprise Commuter (hinterland) and Rural municipalities.

timing.value: migration year t: the last recorded residential move in the calendar year, cross-checked against the following year's registered address

units.value: change in the probability of the outcome per one-unit increase in WFH probability (average marginal effect); the table note states the coefficients should be interpreted as times 100, i.e. in percentage points

estimand.target_population: Residents of Denmark aged 24-74 in primary employment (secondary jobs excluded) living in Copenhagen Capital City Area municipalities (24 municipalities with job accessibility exceeding 200,000), 2014-2023; stayers in the CCA compared with movers from the CCA to rural municipalities
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: the regressor and the migration outcome are both measured for individual i in migration year t

population.description: Residents of Denmark aged 24-74 in primary employment (secondary jobs excluded) living in Copenhagen Capital City Area municipalities (24 municipalities with job accessibility exceeding 200,000), 2014-2023; stayers in the CCA compared with movers from the CCA to rural municipalities
subgroups_defined: occupational skill (manual skilled, high skilled, service skilled)
population.selection: aged 24-74 and in primary employment, secondary jobs excluded; origin municipality in the CCA; the sample contrasts CCA stayers with CCA-to-rural movers

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the estimates come from cross-sectional and between-individual variation in occupation-based WFH probability (and in the demographic and socioeconomic covariates) among CCA residents pooled over 2014-2023, with the model conditioning on a fixed set of controls and year fixed effects. The paper describes itself as an exploratory comparative analysis and its estimates as associations.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the demographic, socioeconomic and locational controls and the year fixed effects, the regressor is independent of the unobserved determinants of the migration outcome, so the reported coefficient can be read as the paper reads it (an effect / an association net of these covariates).

threats_discussed: The post-pandemic window 2022-2023 may be too brief to confirm lasting structural change; the 2022-2023 dynamics are described as still in flux.
Housing types (e.g., detached houses versus flats) are not controlled for; municipal average house prices are used only as a proxy.
Registered residential moves may not capture the full scope of spatial dispersion, such as increased second-home use or temporary relocations.
Denmark's mandatory lockdowns versus Sweden's voluntary mitigation strategy may have affected migration decisions, but this cannot be examined within the scope of the analysis.
Cross-country comparison is complicated by unstandardised urban-rural classifications and remote-work measures.
robustness_checks: Cross-checking the registered residential address in the subsequent year to ensure the move reflects a permanent change in residence (footnote 3, p. 4)

ambiguities: The paper's exhibit titles and narrative use causal language ("effect", "reduces", "mobility shock"), while the empirical-strategy section says the estimates "reflect associations ... net of common yearly fluctuations" and calls the design an exploratory comparative analysis; recorded as identification.strategy = descriptive.
No standard errors, confidence intervals or p-values are printed anywhere in the article; the recorded p-value is the bound implied by the printed significance stars.

No baseline mean of the dependent variable is printed with the regression tables: the article text gives only year ranges (84-88% of Danes remain in the CCA, 11-15% out-migrate, 6-8% of movers go rural; mean rural migration distance about 79 km versus 85 km urban in Denmark), and the descriptive-statistics tables A1 and A2 are not part of the article text.

evidence.how: Read off the significance stars printed with the coefficient together with the table-note legend "***, ** and * indicate significance at the 1%, 5% and 10% level, respectively"; this bounds the p-value and is not an exact p-value printed by the paper.

Cross-country comparison is complicated by unstandardised urban-rural classifications and remote-work measures.

second-home use and temporary relocations, which registered residential moves do not capture
